recipe: Transform all data at the top level of your components rather than using an Effect to update a state variable when props change.
trigger_condition: You need to filter, sort, or otherwise transform data before displaying it in your component.
evidence: To avoid the unnecessary render passes, transform all the data at the top level of your components. That code will automatically re-run whenever your props or state change.
source_name: react.dev learn: You Might Not Need an Effect

recipe: Handle user events in the corresponding event handlers rather than in Effects.
trigger_condition: You need to respond to user interactions such as button clicks or form submissions.
evidence: This is why you'll usually handle user events in the corresponding event handlers.
source_name: react.dev learn: You Might Not Need an Effect

recipe: Use console.time and console.timeEnd to measure whether a calculation is actually expensive enough to warrant memoization before wrapping it in useMemo.
trigger_condition: You are unsure whether a calculation is slow enough to justify adding useMemo.
evidence: If you want to get more confidence, you can add a console log to measure the time spent in a piece of code:

recipe: When a prop changes and you need to reset or adjust a part of your state, delete the Effect and adjust the state directly during rendering by comparing the current prop to a stored previous value.
trigger_condition: You want to reset or adjust a subset of state whenever a specific prop receives a new value.
evidence: Start by deleting the Effect. Instead, adjust the state directly during rendering:

recipe: When adjusting state during rendering, guard the update with a condition comparing the current value to the previous value to avoid infinite re-render loops.
trigger_condition: You are updating state during the render phase using a previous-value pattern.
evidence: A condition like `items !== prevItems` is necessary to avoid loops.
source_name: react.dev learn: You Might Not Need an Effect

recipe: Instead of chaining multiple Effects that each adjust state to trigger the next one, calculate what you can during rendering and consolidate the state adjustments into the relevant event handler.
trigger_condition: You have a chain of Effects where each one adjusts state solely to trigger the next Effect.
evidence: In this case, it's better to calculate what you can during rendering, and adjust the state in the event handler:
source_name: react.dev learn: You Might Not Need an Effect

recipe: When you need the next state value for calculations inside an event handler, define it manually (e.g., `const nextRound = round + 1`) instead of relying on the state variable, which reflects the snapshot at the time of the event.
trigger_condition: You are performing calculations that require the next state value inside a React event handler.
evidence: If you need to use the next value for calculations, define it manually like `const nextRound = round + 1`.
source_name: react.dev learn: You Might Not Need an Effect

recipe: Use a chain of Effects when you cannot calculate the next state directly in an event handler, such as when synchronizing with external data like network responses or dependent form fields.
trigger_condition: The next state depends on data that is not available at the time of the event (e.g., network data, dependent dropdown options).
evidence: a chain of Effects is appropriate because you are synchronizing with network
source_name: react.dev learn: You Might Not Need an Effect

recipe: To run initialization logic exactly once per app load (not per component mount), guard it with a module-level boolean variable checked inside a top-level Effect.
trigger_condition: You have logic that must run only once when the app loads, such as loading from localStorage or checking an auth token.
evidence: add a top-level variable to track whether it has already executed
source_name: react.dev learn: You Might Not Need an Effect

recipe: You can run app-wide initialization during module initialization (before the app renders) by placing it in top-level code with a browser environment check, but keep this pattern limited to root component modules or entry points to avoid slowdown when importing arbitrary components.
trigger_condition: You need initialization logic that runs once per app load and does not depend on component rendering.
evidence: You can also run it during module initialization and before the app renders
source_name: react.dev learn: You Might Not Need an Effect

recipe: Instead of using an Effect to notify a parent component of state changes, delete the Effect and update both the child's and parent's state within the same event handler so React batches them into a single render pass.
trigger_condition: A child component needs to notify its parent of internal state changes (e.g., via an onChange callback) and you are currently doing so in an Effect.
evidence: Delete the Effect and instead update the state of *both* components within the same event handler
source_name: react.dev learn: You Might Not Need an Effect

recipe: Whenever you find yourself trying to keep two different state variables synchronized, lift the state up to a common parent component instead of maintaining separate state in each.
trigger_condition: Two components (or a component and its parent) each hold state that must stay in sync with each other.
evidence: Whenever you try to keep two different state variables synchronized, try lifting state up instead!
source_name: react.dev learn: You Might Not Need an Effect

recipe: Instead of passing data from a child to a parent via an Effect, let the parent component fetch the data and pass it down to the child as a prop to keep data flow predictable and traceable.
trigger_condition: A child component fetches data and passes it up to a parent component through an Effect.
evidence: let the parent component fetch that data, and *pass it down* to the child instead
source_name: react.dev learn: You Might Not Need an Effect

recipe: Replace manual external store subscription in an Effect with a call to `useSyncExternalStore`, wrapping your subscribe/getServerSnapshot/getSnapshot functions in a custom Hook to avoid repeating the code in individual components.
trigger_condition: Your component needs to subscribe to data outside of React state (e.g., a third-party library or a browser API like navigator.onLine).
evidence: Delete the Effect and replace it with a call to [`useSyncExternalStore`](/reference/react/useSyncExternalStore)
source_name: react.dev learn: You Might Not Need an Effect

recipe: Use an Effect for data fetching when you need to keep local state synchronized with network data for the current props, even if the data is not triggered by a user event (e.g., search inputs prepopulated from the URL).
trigger_condition: A component needs to keep its local state in sync with external data (e.g., network results) that depends on its current props.
evidence: While this component is visible, you want to keep `results` [synchronized](/learn/synchronizing-with-effects) with data from the network for the current `page` and `query`. This is why it's an Effect.
source_name: react.dev learn: You Might Not Need an Effect

recipe: To fix race conditions in data fetching Effects, add a cleanup function that sets a flag (e.g., `ignore = true`) so that stale responses from earlier requests are ignored when they arrive after a newer request has been made.
trigger_condition: Your Effect triggers multiple asynchronous requests (e.g., rapid user input) and responses may arrive out of order, causing you to display stale data.
evidence: you need to [add a cleanup function](/learn/synchronizing-with-effects#fetching-data) to ignore stale responses
source_name: react.dev learn: You Might Not Need an Effect

recipe: Keep app-wide initialization logic confined to root component modules (like `App.js`) or your application's entry point rather than scattering it across many components, since top-level code runs once on import even if the component is never rendered.
trigger_condition: You are considering placing top-level (module-scope) initialization code in a component file that may be imported but not rendered.
evidence: Keep app-wide initialization logic to root component modules like `App.js` or in your application's entry point.
source_name: react.dev learn: You Might Not Need an Effect

recipe: If you can calculate something during render, don't use an Effect to update it.
trigger_condition: You find yourself using useEffect to update state that could simply be computed during the render phase.
evidence: If you can calculate something during render, you don't need an Effect.
source_name: react.dev learn: You Might Not Need an Effect

recipe: To cache expensive calculations, add useMemo instead of useEffect.
trigger_condition: A computation is expensive and you need to avoid re-running it on every render.
evidence: To cache expensive calculations, add `useMemo` instead of `useEffect`.
source_name: react.dev learn: You Might Not Need an Effect

recipe: To reset the state of an entire component tree, pass a different key to it.
trigger_condition: You need to reset all internal state of a component subtree from scratch.
evidence: To reset the state of an entire component tree, pass a different `key` to it.
source_name: react.dev learn: You Might Not Need an Effect

recipe: To reset a particular bit of state in response to a prop change, set it during rendering.
trigger_condition: A prop change requires resetting a specific state variable without using an Effect.
evidence: To reset a particular bit of state in response to a prop change, set it during rendering.
source_name: react.dev learn: You Might Not Need an Effect

recipe: Code that runs because a component was displayed should be in Effects, the rest should be in events.
trigger_condition: You are deciding whether to place logic in useEffect or in an event handler.
evidence: Code that runs because a component was *displayed* should be in Effects, the rest should be in events.
source_name: react.dev learn: You Might Not Need an Effect

recipe: If you need to update the state of several components, do it during a single event.
trigger_condition: Multiple components need their state updated in response to the same user action.
evidence: If you need to update the state of several components, it's better to do it during a single event.
source_name: react.dev learn: You Might Not Need an Effect

recipe: Whenever you try to synchronize state variables in different components, consider lifting state up.
trigger_condition: Two or more components need to share or synchronize state variables.
evidence: Whenever you try to synchronize state variables in different components, consider lifting state up.
source_name: react.dev learn: You Might Not Need an Effect

recipe: When fetching data with Effects, implement cleanup to avoid race conditions.
trigger_condition: You are using useEffect to fetch data that depends on changing parameters such as a URL.
evidence: You can fetch data with Effects, but you need to implement cleanup to avoid race conditions.
source_name: react.dev learn: You Might Not Need an Effect

recipe: Extract data fetching logic into a custom Hook to make it easier to adopt an efficient data fetching strategy later.
trigger_condition: You need to fetch data in a component but prefer not to rely on a full framework's built-in data fetching mechanism.
evidence: moving the data fetching logic into a custom Hook will make it easier to adopt an efficient data fetching strategy later.

recipe: Extract a piece of functionality into a custom Hook with a more declarative and purpose-built API whenever you have to resort to writing Effects.
trigger_condition: You find yourself writing complex or repetitive useEffect logic in a component.
evidence: whenever you have to resort to writing Effects, keep an eye out for when you can extract a piece of functionality into a custom Hook with a more declarative and purpose-built API

recipe: Extract state that only affects a small portion of the UI into a separate child component so the parent does not re-render on every keystroke.
trigger_condition: A state variable in a parent component (e.g. a text input) causes the parent to re-render on every change, but that state only affects a small sub-tree of the UI.
evidence: Since the `text` state variable can't possibly affect the list of todos, you can extract the `NewTodo` form into a separate component, and move the `text` state variable inside of it

recipe: To reset a component's internal state when a prop (such as an ID) changes, split the component in two and pass the changing value as the `key` prop to the inner component instead of using `useEffect` to sync state.

evidence: Split the `EditContact` component in two. Move all the form state into the inner `EditForm` component. Export the outer `EditContact` component, and make it pass `savedContact.id` as the `key` to the inner `EditForm` component.
